rv.q: There’s hope to be found in that – and in this richly satisfying evening.
Matthew Warchus' production, performed by an impeccable cast led by Hollywood royalty Susan Sarandon and Andrea Riseborough, could hardly be more finely calibrated.
It is a subtle and elegantly constructed piece of work.
There’s a quiet wisdom to that, beauty in celebrating an “ordinary” life, and the play’s elusiveness suggests it’s hard to know anyone fully.

Sarandon is a catch and it's a play with a gently devastating depth-charge effect. But it's also an evening tinged with frustration at the way it gets snagged on the complexities of its own construction.
Letts wants to let us join the dots for ourselves, but the end result can feel more like a writing exercise than a fully satisfying play.
The round shows Mary from all sides, in theory, yet you do not see her clearly at all.

The good news is that Susan Sarandon is vivid: a relief for those of us braced to watch yet another movie star jetting across the Atlantic to suck the life out of a piece of theatre. The disappointment is the play.
It’s a smart piece of writing that’s given us some fine performances - particularly from Riseborough - but its fussy theatricality ultimately gets in the way.
And if all these bodies somehow fail to fit together into a single living, breathing portrait of an actual person, each still brings some brilliance of its own to this fractured story.
Yet there is a glibness to the way this is largely what transpires.
Life, this lovely play knows full well, doesn't work like that.
In their hands, this odd conceit just about works, creating images of a life both lived and wasted, pre-ordained and chosen.
It is the excellent acting that vividly brings every Mary to life, as Letts asks (but never answers) the eternal question of what is fated to happen in a life and what we can control.
Ultimately, Mary Page Marlowe proves a thoughtful and often moving exploration of a life lived.

Mary Page Marlowe’s time-jumping episodes make sense of the juxtapositions – indeed contradictions – that a life, with or without regrets, and its memories and crossroads, will have and provide an outstanding vehicle for some truly leading ladies of the theatre.
The Mary Page Marlowe you construct may change form as these scenes follow each other, but it can never be a complete picture and that is true to fact.
Not a bad night out, not a great one.
In presenting these human interactions, strengths and frailties, the piece certainly works, but I was left pondering whether it could potentially work more effectively as a movie.
Mary Page Marlowe is an incredible piece of theatre, overall.
You leave with the powerful sense that no life is uninteresting, no matter how well or wastefully lived.
While the staging issues detract slightly from the overall experience, this production remains a moving and thoughtful meditation on identity and memory.
What an extraordinary amount of time, talent and effort has gone into delivering so very little.

cn.t: Critics find Letts' fragmented portrait of one woman's life intriguing but uneven, with Sarandon's magnetic UK stage debut and strong ensemble work elevating material that some find skimpy or unremarkable despite its poignant moments.
